newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dollar calms by late Tokyo after windy session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar calms by late Tokyo after windy session.

text.p: The dollar calmed down by late Tokyo trading on Friday after a windy early session led by inconsistent statements made by government officials.

"An artificial attempt to check a further slide by the yen may not yield any result, given that Japan's low interest rates are pushing Japanese capital abroad," said Kabun Muto, director-general of the Management and Coordination Agency.
Muto's remark drove the dollar up to a high of 126.25 yen.
Most traders expect dollar-selling intervention by the Bank of Japan (BOJ) if the dollar surges to near 127 yen again.
Muto added that there was nothing wrong with the dollar moving above 125 yen, adding that in terms of purchasing-power parity, 150 yen to the dollar would be appropriate.
But those dollar gains were soon pared after a Ministry of Finance official told Reuters: "Muto's remarks regarding the dollar/yen rate do not reflect the official policy of the Japanese government."
"The official view is, as the Finance Minister (Hiroshi Mitsuzuka) said, that the yen's recent falls are overdone and (the ministry) is concerned about it," the MOF official added.
On credit policy, Muto also said the Bank of Japan should increase its official discount rate (ODR) by the end of this year to discourage capital outflows from Japan, he said.
Muto's remark on credit policy also pushed up the yields of Japanese government bonds (JGBs).
But the rise in the JGB yields failed to strengthen the Japanese currency due to lingering dollar-buying interest by institutional investors and local importers, traders said.
BOJ Governor Yasuo Matsushita said on Friday that the central bank does not conduct monetary policy on the basis of foreign interest rates and currency movements alone.

Currency traders said that the only means currently available to check a further slide in the yen would be dollar-selling intervention as a credit tightening does not appear to be on the cards for the BOJ.

"The Bank of Japan is set for an imminent action (dollar-selling intervention), but they will have to do it alone," said Takeshi Hanai, executive manager of Industrial Bank of Japan Ltd's International Treasury Department.
On Thursday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said that he shared Japan's concern about the yen's recent fall, but also reiterated that the strong dollar is in the U.S. interest.
Traders said Rubin's remark implied the Treasury supports BOJ's bid to check a dollar rally, but was reluctant to use its own money.
